phrase: Satoshi Nakamoto has released an official statement
note: Satoshi Nakamoto published the Bitcoin white paper in 2008 and stopped writing publicly in 2011. There is no office that sets the price. The line opens the track as a fake bulletin, with a news desk treating bitcoin like a company that just announced a hike.

A nocoiner holds no bitcoin and usually argues it is unnecessary. The anchor has them upset that holders will not sell. A price still needs someone on the other side of the trade, and the people with the coins declined.

Diamond hands means refusing to sell through a drawdown. "Have been forced" twists the meme: after the 2021–22 bull run, not selling was the culture, and the fake report is really complaining that nobody will provide liquidity.

Harrison Ford's screen image is the person who already walked out with the treasure — Indiana Jones in a temple of gold, then a 1990s star sitting on the result. Early coins, in this bar, are that artifact. Everyone else showed up late to the dig.

Encryption keeps a message or a key unreadable without the secret. The early-2020s self-custody mood was: if a bank can close the account, encrypt the backups and route around it. The bar's tone is refusal. The practice is keeping secrets a government cannot reset.

A satoshi is one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin. Parking them on a USB stick is improvised cold storage — keys offline, not sitting in an exchange account — and "trading amongst the people" is the peer-to-peer part. Lose the stick and the coins are gone. The apostrophes are street grammar. The rule underneath is still: not your keys, not your coins.

phrase: the one with the lowest vax rate
note: Lockdowns were fading by Pizza Day 2023, and red-pill health talk had already mixed into Bitcoin Twitter. A "lowest vax rate" test for which coin survives is that crossover used as a punchline: a fake fundamental, not a metric.

The World Economic Forum is the Davos group associated with Great Reset branding. In maximalist slang, WEF stands for policy shops that want to regulate, surveil, or co-opt the chain. "Legislate" and "attack the chain," in the next bars, are the rest of that complaint.
Proof-of-work electricity use was the standard public attack on Bitcoin through the 2021 bull market, often flattened into a climate slogan. The bar files it under talking smack and moves on.

phrase: Forget electric cars, but where's the free energy at
note: Electric cars were the respectable climate product. "Free energy" is the fringe claim that usable power is being withheld. One line shrugs at both: the consumer fix and the suppressed-technology story.
A tinfoil hat is the cartoon of a conspiracy theorist. Misplacing it because the buying never stopped is a self-roast. The narrator clocks how the rant sounds and keeps going.

Stacking sats means buying small amounts of bitcoin on repeat. One satoshi is 0.00000001 BTC. Calling the habit the biggest drug is the culture admitting the pull is the stack itself, not a single green trade.

Laser eyes on a profile photo were the 2021 maximalist badge, aimed at a bitcoin price of $100,000 and beyond. "21 gazillion Fahrenheit" inflates the bit: 21 echoes the 21 million coin cap, and the temperature is not a forecast.

To orange-pill someone is to convince them of Bitcoin — the red pill, recoloured to Bitcoin orange. A hard pill is the version with no soft landing for nocoiners: fixed supply, self-custody, and no altcoin on the side.

The lyric spells it Weimer. The history is Weimar Germany, where the mark collapsed after World War I and prices outran wages. The lesson, aimed at people in their twenties and at their kids, is what money does when issuance has no cap.

phrase: Chancellor is on brink of their 37th bailout
note: Bitcoin's genesis block, mined 3 January 2009, timestamps a Times headline: "Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks." The fake desk has moved the count to a 37th. Same front page as the chain, stretched into a running gag about rescues that never stop.

phrase: Peter Schiff has liquidated his entire gold portfolio
note: Peter Schiff manages gold and spent years calling Bitcoin a bubble. He did not sell the metal for coins. Inside a song staged as a newscast, that headline is the item that would never run — and the rest of the line has him doing it "in favour of bitcoin."

Silk Road was a darknet market, shut down in 2013, that used Bitcoin as its payment rail. "We got in early" puts some of that era in the narrator's origin story. The drugs tag is the song being blunt about it, not a guide.

phrase: that rug pull you were in explains why you're in retail trying to push rugs
note: A rug pull is when a token's creators remove the liquidity and leave holders with something they cannot sell. The pun walks that person off the crypto rug and onto a shop floor selling actual rugs.
A Lambo was the 2017 cartoon of a trade that worked: a Lamborghini as proof. A Camry is the ordinary car after it did not. The line is the round trip from flex back to normal.
Altcoins are coins other than Bitcoin. A maximalist hears the question as the mistake. The verse refuses it, then labels the whole stretch out loud: "Altcoin reference."

"Toxic maxi" became a mainstream insult after the 2021–22 bull run: a Bitcoin maximalist who will not entertain other coins. "Marginalised white male" is culture-war phrasing laid on top of that. The bar puts the costume on and keeps the verse moving. British spelling and all, it is self-parody.

The keys — a private key, or the seed phrase that derives it — are what can spend bitcoin. Lose them and the coins sit on the chain where nobody can move them. "Not your keys, not your coins" is the usual slogan, and this line is the failure mode. The little piggies in the next bar, whether that means police or anyone else without the seed, cannot get into a house they do not hold the keys to.

Trading proverb: bulls make money, bears make money, pigs get slaughtered. Pigs are the greedy ones who will not get out of a winning trade and get carried off. "Oink oink lessons" is the verse tapping the table before it says so.

A CBDC is a central-bank digital currency: state money that can be identified, frozen, or limited by rule. Bitcoin is not one. "Can't spend them for wifi" is the small version of that worry — a balance that still needs permission before it clears.

Mi goreng is the instant noodle that became an Australian pantry staple: cheap, salty, everywhere. Robbie P is Australian, and the bowl sits between a speech on grocery prices and a penthouse. The fortress fantasy and the student food are in the same verse.

Max Keiser is a Bitcoin broadcaster known for on-air fights with gold advocate Peter Schiff. The bar aims that heckling at nocoiners. "On the end of Bitcoin slang" also points back at Robbie P's earlier Bitcoin Slang track, which already named Schiff.

The citadel is a Bitcoin forum meme from the early 2010s: a walled compound where early holders live above the people who waited. The penthouse of the tallest building inside the fortress is that story told as real estate.

The hook takes the insult and awards him the title. The single landed on Bitcoin Pizza Day 2023 — the third Pizza Day drop in a row — and the video is cut as a fake news report about this character. Pizza Day is 22 May, the date of the 2010 trade of 10,000 BTC for two pizzas.

The desk claims a million dollars a coin moments after a print of $3,400. The 2018 bear market bottomed in the low $3,000s that December, so the figure reads as that scar, not a live quote. The million is the satire turned all the way up.

A slingshot here is a violent reversal: price cracks, then snaps the other way before traders can get out. "Upside" is the snap up. Short positions — bets that profit only if price falls — get annihilated on the way, because liquidation is forced buying, which can shove the price higher still. "Billions across the globe" is the bulletin's volume knob.
